analysis.one_liner: Temporarily blocks class action lawsuits against lenders over Truth in Lending disclosure errors.
analysis.headline: Congress passed the bill by voice vote in both chambers within three weeks of introduction, and the President signed it into law in May 1995, blocking consumer class actions over lender disclosure mistakes until October 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This law put a time-limited moratorium on courts certifying class action lawsuits against creditors under the Truth in Lending Act. It covered claims that a lender mishandled the disclosed finance charge in a mortgage refinancing or consolidation loan, or gave borrowers the wrong form of rescission notice because it picked the wrong model form. A class action is a single lawsuit brought on behalf of many affected borrowers at once; the law stopped courts from approving them for those claims until October 1, 1995, with only narrow exceptions.
analysis.who_benefits: Mortgage lenders and other consumer creditors facing class action lawsuits over disclosure errors gain, because the law blocks courts from certifying those classes during the moratorium window, removing the leverage that a multi-borrower lawsuit gives borrowers and their lawyers.

how_it_helps.text: The law blocks courts from certifying any class in Truth in Lending Act cases involving finance-charge disclosure errors or wrong-form rescission notices in refinancing or consolidation loans secured by a first lien, from enactment until October 1, 1995.

Class actions pool many small individual claims into one lawsuit, which can expose a lender to large damages; blocking certification during the moratorium removes that exposure for the covered claims.

analysis.who_pays: Borrowers with disclosure-error claims against refinancing lenders lose their ability to band together in a class action during the moratorium, leaving only individual suits, which are usually too small to be worth bringing, or the narrow exceptions in the law.

drawbacks.text: During the moratorium, borrowers who were charged undisclosed fees or given the wrong rescission notice form could not join together in a class action; class actions are typically the only practical way to pursue small individual lending violations.

The exceptions are narrow: they preserve class actions only when the misdisclosed finance charge pushes the annual percentage rate beyond the statutory tolerance, when no rescission notice was given in any form, or when the notice failed for reasons other than picking the wrong model form.

The honest case for the bill was that class actions built on technical form-choice errors mostly rewarded lawyers while the underlying disclosure rules stayed the same; the cost of fixing that problem this way was that borrowers with real, uncovered violations also lost their group remedy for the duration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gave lenders relief from a wave of disclosure-error class actions for a fixed window and left the underlying law unchanged afterward. Borrowers bore the cost: for roughly five months they could not use the class action mechanism for covered claims, and the narrow exceptions did not reach many small-disclosure violations. Whether that trade was worth it depends on how much weight you give the argument that such suits mainly compensated attorneys.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote the day after it was introduced under a fast-track procedure, the Senate passed it without amendment by voice vote three weeks later, and the President signed it on May 18, 1995.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 3, 1995, and referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services and several other committees.

The next day, April 4, 1995, Rep. Roukema moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill, a fast-track procedure used for measures leaders consider noncontroversial; the House agreed to it by voice vote.
The Senate passed the bill without amendment by voice vote on April 24, 1995.
The President signed the bill on May 18, 1995, making it Public Law 104-12.

The law adds a class action moratorium to the Truth in Lending Act, barring courts from certifying classes for specified finance-charge and rescission-notice violations in refinancing and consolidation loans until October 1, 1995, subject to narrow exceptions.
The bill's ten cosponsors were all Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and other consumer creditors came out ahead: the law blocked class certification of disclosure-error suits during the moratorium, eliminating that liability exposure, while borrowers lost the ability to pursue those claims as a group.

for.name: Marge Roukema
for.what_they_did: Moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill on the House floor the day after introduction.

for.what_they_did: Passed the bill by voice vote with no recorded opposition, four weeks between introduction and final passage.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on May 18, 1995.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all ten cosponsors were Republicans, but both chambers passed the bill by voice vote with no recorded votes, so the support or opposition of individual members and parties cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The law blocks courts from certifying class actions against them for specified Truth in Lending disclosure and rescission-notice errors during the moratorium, removing their biggest liability exposure on those claims. Borrowers' group remedy is the cost of that gain.

The moratorium stops certification of the covered class actions, eliminating fee and recovery opportunities in those cases for the duration. Their interest ran with borrowers', since the suits were the borrowers' remedy.
